surveyDefinition.title: Smartwatches — consumer survey (India)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on smartwatch ownership and usage patterns, purchase drivers, feature priorities, and future upgrade intentions.

segments.name: Health-Focused Users
segments.description: Own a smartwatch primarily for continuous health and fitness tracking—steps, heart rate, sleep, and advanced metrics. They use the device daily, often during workouts and overnight, and are willing to pay more for accuracy and actionable insights.

segments.name: Value-Driven Family
segments.description: Purchase smartwatches for themselves or family members for basic health tracking, notifications, and safety. They are price-sensitive, seek durability and ease of use, and are less interested in advanced or premium features.

segments.name: Style-Led Owners
segments.description: Wear a smartwatch as a fashion accessory as much as a functional device. They value customization, aesthetics, and brand image, and are willing to pay for premium materials and interchangeable bands.

segments.name: Tech-Savvy Early Adopters
segments.description: Own the latest smartwatches and are driven by new technology, advanced sensors, and ecosystem integration. They are early adopters, less price-sensitive, and frequently upgrade to gain new capabilities.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Smartwatches buyers in India. It asks how people use Smartwatches, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in India who buy or use Smartwatches for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who currently own or have purchased a smartwatch in the past 12 months; Individuals who are actively considering purchasing a smartwatch within the next 6 months; Adults aged 18+ who make their own purchase decisions. Excluded: Businesses or institutions purchasing smartwatches in bulk for employees; Children under 18 (unless the study specifically targets kids' smartwatches, which is not the primary market); Individuals who only use basic fitness bands without smart features.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model and brand themselves. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining purchase is by individual consumers, making this a pure B2C market.
respondentBehaviours: Health and fitness tracking (steps, heart rate, sleep)
Smartphone integration for notifications and calls
Brand loyalty to smartphone ecosystems (Apple, Samsung, etc.)
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how they use it day-to-day, then moves into the purchase journey—what triggered the buy, where they researched, and what decided the choice. It then explores what they now expect from the device, including must-have features and trade-offs, and closes with satisfaction, frustrations, and future upgrade intentions. This arc separates the four segments by their usage depth, purchase drivers, feature priorities, and upgrade behaviour.

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Smartwatches in India — who Individuals who currently own or have purchased a smartwatch in the past 12 months; Individuals who are actively considering purchasing a smartwatch within the next 6 months; Adults aged 18+ who make their own purchase decisions. The audience is defined as individual consumers who buy smartwatches for personal use, as they are the primary purchasers and decision-makers. The demographic and behavioral criteria capture both current owners and potential buyers to support a broad consumer survey.

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on smartwatch ownership and usage patterns, purchase drivers, feature priorities, and future upgrade intentions.

segments.name: Health-Focused Users
segments.description: Own a smartwatch primarily for continuous health and fitness tracking—steps, heart rate, sleep, and advanced metrics. They use the device daily, often during workouts and overnight, and are willing to pay more for accuracy and actionable insights.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report the highest usage frequency, prioritize sensor accuracy and battery life for all-day tracking, and show strong interest in advanced health features like blood pressure or ECG.

segments.name: Value-Driven Family
segments.description: Purchase smartwatches for themselves or family members for basic health tracking, notifications, and safety. They are price-sensitive, seek durability and ease of use, and are less interested in advanced or premium features.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report moderate usage, emphasize price and durability in purchase decisions, and be more likely to consider mid-range or older models.

segments.name: Style-Led Owners
segments.description: Wear a smartwatch as a fashion accessory as much as a functional device. They value customization, aesthetics, and brand image, and are willing to pay for premium materials and interchangeable bands.
segments.hypothesis: This group will prioritize design and customization options over technical specs, and will be more likely to switch brands for a more elegant or fashionable model.

segments.name: Tech-Savvy Early Adopters
segments.description: Own the latest smartwatches and are driven by new technology, advanced sensors, and ecosystem integration. They are early adopters, less price-sensitive, and frequently upgrade to gain new capabilities.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report the highest spend, shortest upgrade cycles, and strong interest in cutting-edge features like blood glucose monitoring or AI coaching.

segmentModel.tie_break: Question cp6 (main reason you wear your smartwatch) is the most direct behavioural self-report that cleanly separates all four segments by their primary motivation—health tracking, notifications/safety, style, or tech features.
notes: Practical family buyers are primarily identified through purchase context (gift, sale) and price sensitivity, with fewer usage-based signals.
Tech enthusiasts are identified through recency of purchase, latest model ownership, and willingness to pay for new technology.
Health optimizers are strongly identified through continuous wear, sleep/workout tracking, and willingness to pay for accuracy.
Style-led owners are identified through fashion-related wear contexts, design priorities, and material concerns.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing who owns a smartwatch and how they use it day-to-day, then moves into the purchase journey—what triggered the buy, where they researched, and what decided the choice. It then explores what they now expect from the device, including must-have features and trade-offs, and closes with satisfaction, frustrations, and future upgrade intentions. This arc separates the four segments by their usage depth, purchase drivers, feature priorities, and upgrade behaviour.
storyline_notes: Added a beat on feature engagement in the usage section to separate heavy health users from casual notification-checkers.
Included a dedicated battery and comfort beat in preferences, as battery life is a top pain point across all personas.
Placed price paid in the buying section and value expectation in preferences to capture both actual spend and perceived value.
Added a switching triggers beat in the final section to identify what would push each segment to a different brand.
Reflected the Asia Pacific region by including mobile-first research and online marketplace channels in the discovery and purchase beats.
Kept all beats answerable with closed questions and avoided asking age, income, or geography directly.
metadata.classification_reason: Consumers buy smartwatches for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the model and brand themselves. While some businesses may purchase smartwatches for employees, the dominant and defining purchase is by individual consumers, making this a pure B2C market.
